x.ASV: A Psalm of David. Jehovah saith unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, Until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
x.Darby: Psalm of David. Jehovah said unto my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I put thine enemies [as] footstool of thy feet.
x.KJV: A Psalm of David. The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
x.YLT: A Psalm of David. The affirmation of Jehovah to my Lord: `Sit at My right hand, Till I make thine enemies thy footstool.'

nt: Yahweh is using **Sit at my right hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Take the place of highest honor and authority beside me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Sit with me in the honored place]

Here Yahweh is speaking of defeating enemies as if he were making them into **a footstool for your feet**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [until I give you victory over your enemies]

x.ASV: Jehovah will send forth the rod of thy strength out of Zion: Rule thou in the midst of thine enemies.
x.Darby: Jehovah shall send the sceptre of thy might out of Zion: rule in the midst of thine enemies.
x.KJV: The Lord shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies.
x.YLT: The rod of thy strength doth Jehovah send from Zion, Rule in the midst of thine enemies.

nt: Here, **scepter** represents royal authority and power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will expand the area where you strongly rule]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **scepter** that is characterized by **strength**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your strong scepter]

The word translated as **rule** is an imperative, but it communicates an invitation to rule rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate an invitation for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates an invitation. Alternate translation: [I want you to rule]

x.ASV: Thy people offer themselves willingly In the day of thy power, in holy array: Out of the womb of the morning Thou hast the dew of thy youth.
x.Darby: Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power, in holy splendour: from the womb of the morning [shall come] to thee the dew of thy youth.
x.KJV: Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power, in the beauties of holiness from the womb of the morning: thou hast the dew of thy youth.
x.YLT: Thy people are free-will gifts in the day of Thy strength, in the honours of holiness, From the womb, from the morning, Thou hast the dew of thy youth.

nt: David is speaking of **Your people** as if they were **freewill offerings**. He means that the people will willingly offer themselves to serve the king, just as people willingly bring offerings to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your people are like freewill offerings]

David is using this possessive form **the day of your strength** to mean when you show how strong you are. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [when you show how strong you are]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **beauty** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in holy beauty]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **beauty** and **holiness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [they will be beautiful and holy] or [because they are holy, they will be beautiful]

Here David is speaking of the king’s youthful vigor as if it were **the dew of your youth** that comes **from the womb of the dawn**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you will be as fresh as the dew that comes early every morning]

x.ASV: Jehovah hath sworn, and will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever After the order of Melchizedek.
x.Darby: Jehovah hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art priest for ever after the order of Melchisedek.
x.KJV: The Lord hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.
x.YLT: Jehovah hath sworn, and doth not repent, `Thou art a priest to the age, According to the order of Melchizedek.'

nt: The pronoun **it** refers to the oath or solemn promise that Yahweh has made and that David is about to repeat. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and will not revoke this oath]

x.ASV: The Lord at thy right hand Will strike through kings in the day of his wrath.
x.Darby: The Lord at thy right hand will smite through kings in the day of his anger.
x.KJV: The Lord at thy right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath.
x.YLT: The Lord on thy right hand smote kings In the day of His anger.

nt: David is using **at your right hand** as a common expression of his culture to mean “near you to help you” or “fighting for you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The Lord is near you to help you]
David assumes that readers will know that **The Lord** refers to Yahweh. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is]

Here David is speaking as if the Lord were a person who physically **crushes kings**. He means that the Lord defeats enemy kings. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He defeats enemy kings]

David is using the phrase **the day of his nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean that the Lord is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on the day of his anger] or [when he displays his anger]

x.ASV: He will judge among the nations, He will fill the places with dead bodies; He will strike through the head in many countries.
x.Darby: He shall judge among the nations; he shall fill [all places] with dead bodies; he shall smite through the head over a great country.
x.KJV: He shall judge among the heathen, he shall fill the places with the dead bodies; he shall wound the heads over many countries.
x.YLT: He doth judge among the nations, He hath completed the carcases, Hath smitten the head over the mighty earth.

nt: By **He will judge the nations**, David means that Yahweh will punish the nations for their wickedness. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He will punish the nations]

Here, **the nations** represents the people who live in the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people living in many nations]

By **he fills with bodies**, David means he fills the battlefield with dead bodies. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he fills the battlefield with dead bodies]

David is not referring to a specific **head**. He means the heads of the king’s enemies in general. The word translated as **head** could refer to: (1) the heads of the enemy soldiers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh crushes the heads of the enemy soldiers] or (2) the leaders of the enemy armies. Alternate translation: [Yahweh defeats the leaders of the enemy armies]
The word translated as **land** could refer to: (1) a battlefield. Alternate translation: [on a large battlefield] or (2) the earth. Alternate translation: [over the whole earth]

x.ASV: He will drink of the brook in the way: Therefore will he lift up the head.
x.Darby: He shall drink of the brook in the way; therefore shall he lift up the head.
x.KJV: He shall drink of the brook in the way: therefore shall he lift up the head.
x.YLT: From a brook in the way he drinketh, Therefore he doth lift up the head!

nt: Here, **He** could refer to: (1) the king. Alternate translation: [The king will drink] or (2) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will drink]

**Therefore** introduces the result of Yahweh fighting for and strengthening the king, as the previous verses of this psalm describe. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Because Yahweh has fought for him]

David is using **he will lift up the head** as a common expression of his culture to mean “he will triumph over his enemies.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will triumph over his enemies]
